candidates.name: Single-Arm Cable Fly (Standing)

distinctFrom.why: unilateral loading; working side must resist trunk rotation the bilateral fly does not demand

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (unilateral training chapter)
candidates.notes: One handle, one pulley height; anti-rotation demand at the trunk is the reason to programme it, not extra chest stimulus.

candidates.name: Decline Cable Chest Press

distinctFrom.why: bench angle reversed (decline vs incline) changes the pressing vector and shifts emphasis toward lower chest fibres

sources: ACSM Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription (resistance training chapter)
candidates.notes: Bench-based, mirrors the existing Incline Cable Chest Press row (which derives to lying); named without "(Standing)" to avoid implying a standing decline press, which is not how this is performed.

candidates.name: Incline Cable Chest Press (Single-Arm)

distinctFrom.why: unilateral loading; one side presses while the other stabilises, adding an anti-rotation core demand the bilateral version does not have

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (unilateral training chapter)
candidates.notes: Bench-based like the bilateral row it is distinct from; derives to lying, matching that row.

candidates.name: Cable Squeeze Press (Chest)

distinctFrom.why: new movement family for this corpus: two independent handles pressed/squeezed together at chest height for a medial (adduction) emphasis, distinct from the arcing pattern of a fly and from a plate-based Svend Press

sources: Contreras, B. & Schoenfeld, B. — applied hypertrophy programming articles (pec isolation/peak-contraction techniques)
candidates.notes: Standing at a cable crossover, two D-handles pressed together in front of the chest; the name-rule deriver returns both position and balanceDemand null for this new pattern, so both are curated here.

candidates.name: Seated Cable Row (Rope)

distinctFrom.why: rope attachment lets the hands rotate and separate at the finish, adding external rotation and a longer contraction the fixed V-handle/bar does not give

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Same station as Seated Cable Row, different attachment; grip rotation at the finish is the mechanical difference EL-2 requires.

candidates.name: Standing Cable Row (Single-Arm)

distinctFrom.why: standing removes the seat/thigh-pad brace the seated version uses, adding hip and core stabilisation against the single-side pull

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (unilateral training chapter)
candidates.notes: The name-rule deriver classifies any "cable row" name as a seated station (existing Single-Arm Cable Row also derives seated); this row is deliberately standing, so position/balanceDemand are curated to avoid inheriting that seated-station default.

candidates.name: Behind-the-Neck Lat Pulldown

distinctFrom.why: bar pulled behind the head/neck rather than to the chest changes the shoulder path to an externally rotated, extended position with materially higher impingement risk

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (contraindicated/high-risk exercise variants discussion)
candidates.notes: never_auto per EL-5 (technical-complexity/injury-risk movement, searchable only). The grip-none name-rule (built for isolated neck-training rows) false-positives on the word "neck" in this name; gripDemand is curated back to bar because this is a loaded pulldown, not neck-harness work.

candidates.name: Rope Lat Pulldown

distinctFrom.why: rope attachment allows the hands to separate and rotate through the pull, unlike the fixed reverse-grip bar; a materially different hand path at the bottom of the rep

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Distinct attachment identity from the existing wide/close/neutral/reverse bar pulldowns.

candidates.name: Cross-Body Cable Lateral Raise

distinctFrom.why: pulley crosses in front of the body from the opposite low pulley, giving a longer stretch and more resistance at the bottom of the rep than a same-side raise

sources: Schoenfeld, B. "Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy" (lateral raise resistance-profile discussion)
candidates.notes: Distinct resistance profile at the bottom of the rep vs the existing same-side low-pulley and behind-the-back variants.

candidates.name: Single-Arm Cable Front Raise

distinctFrom.why: unilateral loading adds an anti-lateral-flexion core demand the bilateral raise does not require

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning (unilateral training chapter)
candidates.notes: Laterality is the only difference from the existing bilateral row; subregion left null (front_delts carries no subregion values in the current seed).

candidates.name: Cable Shoulder Press (Standing)

distinctFrom.why: new movement family for this corpus: no cable overhead-press row exists for front_delts today. Dual low pulleys pressed overhead give constant tension through the full range unlike a machine or free-weight press

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Fills a genuine gap: the cable family has a front raise but no press for front_delts.

candidates.name: Single-Arm Cable Curl (Low Pulley)

distinctFrom.why: unilateral loading at a fixed low pulley, distinct from the two-hand bar/rope curl already in the corpus

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Standard single-arm cable curl; low-pulley position keeps constant tension through the top of the rep unlike a dumbbell curl.

candidates.name: Cable Drag Curl

distinctFrom.why: the bar is dragged up the torso with elbows kept back rather than swinging forward, shifting tension differently through the range and reducing front-delt involvement

sources: Schoenfeld, B. "Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy" (bar path/tension-curve discussion)
candidates.notes: Named bar path (drag) is the mechanical difference from a standard curl, per EL-2.

candidates.name: Cable Incline Curl

distinctFrom.why: performed seated on an incline bench rather than lying flat/prone; the bench angle changes shoulder extension and the point of peak stretch

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Derives to "lying" under the corpus’s incline-movement convention (the position enum has no separate reclined-incline bucket); consistent with how the deriver treats other incline movements.

candidates.name: Cable Pushdown (V-Bar)

distinctFrom.why: angled V-bar handle changes wrist/forearm angle and hand spacing versus the straight bar and rope attachments already in the corpus

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Distinct attachment from the existing straight-bar and rope pushdowns.

candidates.name: Overhead Cable Tricep Extension (Bar)

distinctFrom.why: fixed straight/EZ-bar handle keeps the wrists in a set position through the stretch, unlike the rope which allows the hands to rotate and separate

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Bar-attachment counterpart to the existing rope overhead extension.

candidates.name: Cable Hip Flexion (Standing)

distinctFrom.why: new movement family for this corpus: an ankle cuff at a low pulley raising the knee/hip into flexion, distinct from every squat/press/extension row already filed under quads

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: quads carries no subregion values in the current seed, so subregion is left null.

candidates.name: Cable Romanian Deadlift

distinctFrom.why: new implement family for the hinge pattern under hamstrings: a low-pulley RDL keeps constant tension through the hip hinge, unlike the free-weight barbell/dumbbell RDL

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Fills a genuine gap: no hinge-pattern cable row exists for hamstrings/glutes today, only the isolation leg curl and the glute-filed pull-through.

candidates.name: Standing Cable Crunch

distinctFrom.why: performed standing at a high pulley rather than kneeling/on the floor, removing the floor-contact and hip-flexion component the existing kneeling/floor rows have

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: The word "crunch" trips the name-rule’s lying/floor-access defaults (built for the floor and kneeling crunch rows); this variant is standing at a cable station, so position/floorAccess/balanceDemand are curated.

candidates.name: Standing Calf Raise (Cable)

distinctFrom.why: new implement family for calves: standing on a block or plate attached to a low pulley for constant-tension calf work, distinct from every machine/dumbbell/bodyweight calf row already in the corpus

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: Less common than the machine/dumbbell calf raise but attested as a constant-tension alternative in commercial-gym coaching practice.

candidates.name: Cable Tibialis Raise (Seated)

distinctFrom.why: new implement family for tibialis: seated, cable/band resistance around the forefoot for dorsiflexion, distinct from the machine tibialis rows already in the corpus

sources: NSCA Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning
candidates.notes: tibialis carries no subregion values in the current seed, so subregion is left null.

rejected.name: Kneeling Lat Pulldown
rejected.reason: unattested (standard lat pulldown stations are not set up for a kneeling position; no authoritative source found for this as a distinct standard variant)

rejected.name: Cable Curl (EZ-Bar Attachment)
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 (attachment swap does not materially change the curl versus the existing 'Cable Curl' row)

rejected.name: Cable Rope Front Raise
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 (rope vs bar/handle does not materially change a front raise's mechanics)

rejected.name: Cable Step-Up
rejected.reason: not representable (step-ups are not a standard cable-station movement; no authoritative source found)

rejected.name: Cable Lunge
rejected.reason: not representable (lunges are standardly loaded via barbell/dumbbell/bodyweight; no authoritative source for a cable-loaded lunge as a standard variant)

rejected.name: Cable Reverse Crunch
rejected.reason: not representable (reverse crunch loading is standardly bodyweight or a held plate, not a cable-station movement)

rejected.name: Cable Face Pull (High Pulley) / (Low Pulley)
rejected.reason: not distinct under EL-2 given the existing 'Face Pull' / 'Cable Face Pull' / 'Cable Face Pull (Rope)' cluster is already near-redundant; splitting further by pulley height risks compounding that rather than adding a real distinction

rejected.name: Standing Cable Neck Extension
rejected.reason: not representable (no standard cable-stack attachment for neck extension; the corpus’s neck work uses a harness or dedicated neck machine)

rejected.name: Incline Cable Fly (Single-Arm)
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Single-Arm Cable Fly (Standing)' (adding a separate pulley-height variant for the unilateral fly is granularity the bilateral fly family does not need)

rejected.name: Cable Concentration Curl (Standing)
rejected.reason: duplicate of 'Cable Concentration Curl' (already in the corpus, seated/kneeling by convention; a standing variant is not a materially different exercise)
